title: A Preliminary Analysis of the Botany, Zoology, and Mineralogy of the Voynich Manuscript
authors: Arthur O. Tucker and Rexford H. Talbert
summary: Two botanists match plants, animals and a mineral in the manuscript's drawings to species of 16th-century New Spain, compare some glyphs with the Nahuatl and Spanish handwriting of the Codex Osuna (1563-1566), and propose that the text is a now-extinct dialect of Nahuatl written with a syllabary or alphabet derived from that hand. They read a handful of plant labels as Nahuatl, Mixtec or Spanish loan-word names. The original herbalgram.org copy is no longer served; the url is the Internet Archive copy of the ABC's own PDF.
established: The authors identify 37 plants, 6 animals and 1 mineral in the drawings with species they place in post-Conquest Mexico and neighbouring regions; the identifications are visual comparisons with 16th-century sources such as the Codex Cruz-Badianus (1552) and Hernandez, and the authors say many still need refinement.

They compare a few glyph shapes (a broken 'tl', a backward 's', a 'z') with letterforms in the Codex Osuna and propose a preliminary syllabary/alphabet from them; they state that they are botanists and horticulturists, not linguists, and that the syllabary is a first attempt.

From 'tl' and 'chi' endings in their label readings and from the mix of Classical Nahuatl, Mixtec and Spanish loan-words, they place the proposed dialect in central or northern Mexico, and suggest its speakers may have died in the 16th-century epidemics.

open.question: Does a substitution or syllabic key into Nahuatl, scored on held-out pages, read the manuscript better than its decoys? The proposal names the language but gives no complete key; it needs a Nahuatl corpus on the grid first. Openly licensed text: no period transcription of the Florentine Codex or Cantares Mexicanos is known to me under an explicit open license at a stable plain-text url; public-domain 19th-century editions with Nahuatl text exist (Brinton, Ancient Nahuatl Poetry, 1887, Project Gutenberg #12219, of the order of 100,000 Nahuatl characters mixed with English), and modern Nahuatl Wikipedia (cc-by-sa, a few million characters, mixed modern orthographies) is the large fallback.
open.check: Add a Nahuatl corpus (kind corpus), then score a Nahuatl x substitution key on the hidden pages.

open.question: What are the linguistic affinities of the proposed dialect to extant Nahuatl dialects, and is it truly extinct? (The authors leave this open.)

The authors themselves ask how parchment that may date to the first half of the 15th century came to be used over a century later for a 16th-century Mexican text. Independently of that: can the claimed New World identifications (37 of 303 plants, the six principal animals, the one mineral) be confirmed blind on the scans by independent annotators?
open.check: Blinded identification of the cited plant folios against the proposed species, filed as anchors.
